cells.tense: You are holding the arrangement together by adjusting it, here, as it goes
cells.act: keep the ritual and give it room to change
cells.ask: Pick a practice you keep — a standing meal, a yearly thing, a way of checking in — and change one piece of it on purpose, then keep it going that way.
cells.core:
Where the pattern gets set, you're doing the working version: reading what's before you, adding what's missing, taking out what's gone stale, without announcing it. Things hold because you keep adjusting them, not because they were fixed once.

That same hand can carry something forward. Pick a practice you keep — a standing meal, a yearly thing, a way of checking in — and change one piece of it on purpose, so the shape still fits the life it's in now. You're not guarding it from change and not tearing it up. Keeping it alive by letting it move is the work, and the middle you keep finding for yourself runs on the same skill that keeps a shared thing breathing.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the pattern alive by adjusting it as you go.
cells.verb: finding the middle that keeps moving — adding, subtracting, blending as you go
cells.place: where the pattern gets set — the place where the standing arrangement is made and remade

cells.tense: You are smoothing things before the hard part can be said
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Bring the tension you've been smoothing past into the open with the person it concerns, then follow where that pulls and stay with what comes.
cells.core:
You can feel a disagreement forming and you get there first — adjusting, blending, finding the version that can be lived with. From inside, it feels like keeping the peace. From where they sit, it may show as things not quite landing: rough edges get sanded before anyone can hold them, and some things that need saying keep not getting said.

Harmony built before the conflict arrives isn't harmony, it's a lid. What you actually want is under the thing you keep smoothing. So bring that tension into the open with the person it involves — not as a charge, as information. Then follow where it pulls you and stay present while it does. The adjustment that follows will be real, because it will have something real to adjust to.
cells.sheetLine: You smooth things before they've been said, and the smoothing has a cost.

cells.tense: You have been scattered by engagements, still standing at a door already behind you
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Stay with a person while they're in something hard, ten minutes, without fixing it or taking it on — then stay in touch after.
cells.core:
Each encounter pulls you off your own center — a conversation, a request, a mood that comes in — and by the time you notice, you've been carried somewhere. The adjusting that used to be a skill has become the whole terrain. It's hard to say what you'd choose if nothing were pulling, because something is pulling.

You don't get your center back by trying harder to hold it. You get it back in contact. Sit with a person while they're in something difficult — no advice, no managing it, no absorbing it. Be there, keep your own edges, and let yourself be reached by what they're carrying without taking it over. That's the practice: feeling it with them while staying yourself. Do that once and something in you settles, because you've shown you can be in contact and still be here.

cells.tense: You are setting the pattern that gets followed and calling it just how things are
cells.act: learn how the people before you did it
cells.ask: Find out how a thing you keep was done before you got here — how it started, why anyone bothered — then let what you learn change a detail of how you do it now.
cells.core:
The arrangements hold because you keep them holding — you adjust, you read the moment, you keep the thing going — and if someone asked, you'd say that's just how it works. The adjusting is real. The hand doing it hasn't come up for air in a while.

Go back before you. Find out how a practice you keep was done by the people who kept it before — how it started, what it looked like then, why anyone bothered. Not to restore it, just to know. What you find will tell you something the current version has been carrying without saying so. Then change one detail of how you do it now, informed by what you learned. You'll have a reason for the adjustment instead of just a reflex. The thing gets a maker's name on it — and the name is yours.
